transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, so... I guess I'm here because my job basically told me I needed to come. I do general maintenance and repair work—have for years, really—and I've always worked hard. But lately, well, it’s just gotten to the point where it’s a massive problem. 

I keep forgetting things I’m supposed to do. Like, I’ll have scheduled callbacks with vendors or tenants, or someone will hand me a work order for a busted unit or a leaky sink, and I’ll tell them I'll be right back with the parts, and then... I just completely forget. Even basic follow-ups I promised people to their faces just vanish from my brain the second I walk away to do something else. 

And, I mean, it’s not like I’m doing it on purpose, but the paperwork and the unfinished tickets have just piled up so much. It's incredibly embarrassing. My boss actually pulled me into the office about it. They basically sent me here because there's a chance for me to get promoted soon, but they flat out told me that if I don't get this under control, I'm going to lose my shot at moving up. And I really, really want that position, I've been there a long time and I know how to fix the equipment, it's just... I don't know why I can't just keep these work orders straight in my head like everyone else does, you know? It just feels like a mess.
Do you also find yourself forgetting things in other parts of your life, like appointments, personal tasks, or conversations, or does this mostly happen at work?

Honestly, I don't really know if I do. I haven't really noticed it outside of work, to be completely fair. 

I mean, my life outside the property is pretty quiet, you know? When I finally clock out—which is usually around 5:30, sometimes 6:00 if I get stuck snaking a main drain line or something right at the end of the day—I'm just dead tired. I go home, I kick my boots off, and I don't really have a lot of big schedules to keep track of. It's not like work where there's a clipboard and a radio buzzing every five minutes with some tenant complaining about their radiator knocking again. At home, it's just my own stuff. 

If I forget to, I don't know, take the trash out to the curb on Tuesday night, it just waits until Wednesday. Nobody is pulling me into an office or writing me up for it. And I don't really have a ton of personal appointments anyway. Like, I haven't been to the dentist in probably three years, which I know I should go, but that's not because I forgot an appointment I made, I just never got around to making one in the first place. My sister usually calls me if there's a family thing, so I don't have to remember birthdays or anything like that, she just tells me when to show up. 

So, yeah, I really only notice this whole brain-wipe thing when I'm on the clock. Because at work, there are actual consequences, and the stakes are just so high for me right now. Like I was saying about that promotion, it's a lead supervisor role, which means even more paperwork and coordinating with the contractors. If I can't even remember to order the right HVAC filters for the seasonal changeover when it's just me doing it... well, you see why they're worried. But at home? No, I don't think so. There's just no pressure to remember much of anything, so if I am forgetting things, it hasn't caused any disasters.
Do you find it hard to focus or stay concentrated on tasks, even when they’re important or when you’re trying your best?

Oh, God, yes. All the time. And it drives me absolutely crazy because I really *am* trying my best. It's not for lack of trying, I promise you that. 

Like, we use this digital system for our work orders now. It used to be paper tickets on a clipboard, which had its own problems, but a couple of years ago management gave us all these company tablets. So, I’ll pull up a new digital work order, right? And I’m looking at it, telling myself, okay, I’ve got this, let me just see what the issue is so I can grab my tools. 

But I’ll start reading the notes the office put in, and I’m staring right at the screen, but halfway through the paragraph, my brain just... completely checks out. It just slips right off. I'll hear a landscaping truck backing up outside with that beeping noise, or an air compressor kicking on, or I’ll just suddenly start thinking about a completely different job—like whether I remembered to grab the right size PVC primer for a pipe repair I need to do across the complex later. And then I’ll snap back to the tablet in my hand, and I’ll realize I have absolutely no earthly idea what I just looked at. 

I mean, I literally just read the words with my own two eyes, but none of it stuck. I'll have no clue if the ticket was for a jammed garbage disposal or a busted thermostat. So then I have to start over. And sometimes I do it again! I'll read it a second time and still get distracted by someone's TV playing through a wall or just my own thoughts jumping ahead to the next thing. It's like my brain just refuses to hold onto the information no matter how hard I'm squinting at the screen trying to force myself to focus on it. It takes me ten minutes sometimes just to figure out what tool bag I need to grab, and it's just... it's exhausting, honestly. I just want to be able to read a simple paragraph and go do my job.
Lately, have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even outside of work?

No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm definitely stressed out about the job and this whole promotion thing, but I don't feel hopeless or anything like that. I'm not sitting around crying or feeling down in the dumps, you know? It's just the frustration of my brain not cooperating with me when I need it to. 

Outside of work, things are pretty much the same as they've always been. Like I said, I don't have a wildly exciting life, but I still like doing the things I do. I still enjoy tinkering with stuff in my garage on the weekends. Just this past Saturday, I spent like four hours completely taking apart my old lawnmower carburetor because it was running a little rich, and I actually had a really good time doing it. I put on some classic rock, got my hands dirty, and just kind of lost myself in it. I didn't even realize how much time had passed until my neighbor came over to ask if he could borrow my leaf blower. 

So, I definitely still enjoy my hobbies and messing around with small engines and stuff. I still like watching my shows in the evening. It's not like I've lost the spark for life or anything. It's really just this... this wall I keep hitting when I'm on the clock, trying to keep track of twenty different work orders and remember who I promised what to. That's what's getting to me. But as far as feeling depressed or losing interest in my own life? No, I don't think so. I just want to get this work stuff sorted out so I can actually get that lead supervisor spot and stop feeling like I'm letting everybody down at the complex.
Looking back, did you have similar issues with forgetfulness or trouble focusing when you were in school or doing other tasks as a child?

Oh, wow, going way back... you know, it's funny you ask that, because I was just thinking the other day about how much this whole situation reminds me of when I was a kid. Honestly, yes. I remember being exactly this way back in grade school. And that was, gosh, long before I ever had to worry about work orders or property management or any of the job pressure I'm dealing with right now. 

I mean, if you looked at my old report cards—my mom kept them all in this big plastic tote bin in her basement, bless her heart—every single one of them basically said the exact same thing year after year. The teachers would always write notes to my parents saying that I was a really bright girl, that I had a lot of potential, but... well, there was always a "but." It was always, "but she needs to apply herself," or "she needs to pay closer attention." Because I was constantly, and I mean *constantly*, misplacing my papers. I’d actually do the homework, I swear I would, sitting right there at the kitchen table the night before, and then the next morning it was just... gone. Swallowed by my backpack or stuffed into the wrong folder. We had those old wooden desks where the top lifted up, you know? And the inside of mine was always just an absolute disaster zone of crumpled up worksheets and half-eaten erasers. 

And following directions? Oh, man. The teacher would stand up at the chalkboard and give us three things to do, like, "Read the short story, answer the five questions on the board, and then bring your paper to my desk." I would hear the first part, maybe the second part, and then my brain would just be out the window watching the custodian mow the grass outside or something. I'd miss whole parts of the directions. I'd get through one question and then just start doodling in the margins or trying to take apart my pen to see how the spring worked. 

The teachers were always having to walk down the aisle and tap on my desk, like, "Earth to you, are you going to finish that classwork today?" I needed so many reminders just to get through a standard spelling worksheet that took everyone else ten minutes. I'd just be sitting there staring into space until somebody snapped me out of it. So, yeah, this isn't really a new thing at all. It's just that back then, the worst that happened was I had to stay inside during recess to finish my math, whereas now I might lose a major promotion over it, you know? But the actual brain-wandering, losing-track-of-things part? That’s been there since I was in pigtails, absolutely.
